::: {.objectives}
**Goals.** Compute and plot step lengths, turning angles and speeds;
demonstrate that they depend on the sampling interval; use NSD to diagnose
movement strategy; estimate home ranges with MCP, KDE and AKDE; and show
yourself the autocorrelation problem.

**Time:** ~55 minutes. **Packages:** `amt`, `dplyr`, `tidyr`, `lubridate`,
`ctmm`.
:::


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(amt)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(lubridate)
```
:::


## Setup — the cleaned track from Class 3


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
clean <- read.csv("data/buffalo_kruger.csv.gz") |>
  transmute(id = individual.local.identifier,
            t  = as.POSIXct(timestamp, tz = "UTC"),
            x  = location.long, y = location.lat) |>
  filter(!is.na(x), !is.na(y)) |>
  distinct(id, t, .keep_all = TRUE)

trk <- make_track(clean, x, y, t, id = id, crs = 4326) |>
  transform_coords(crs_to = 32736)

resample_by_id <- function(tr, rate, tol) {
  tr |>
    nest(data = -id) |>
    mutate(data = lapply(data, \(d) {
      d |> track_resample(rate = rate, tolerance = tol) |>
        filter_min_n_burst(min_n = 3)
    })) |>
    unnest(cols = data)
}

trk_hr <- resample_by_id(trk, hours(1), minutes(10))
nrow(trk_hr)
#> [1] 22828
```
:::


## Task 1 — Steps, angles and speeds


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
st <- trk_hr |>
  nest(data = -id) |>
  mutate(data = lapply(data, steps_by_burst)) |>
  unnest(cols = data)

st <- st |> mutate(speed_kmh = (sl_ / 1000) / as.numeric(dt_, units = "hours"))

st |>
  summarise(n = n(),
            median_sl = round(median(sl_)),
            q99_sl = round(quantile(sl_, 0.99)),
            max_sl = round(max(sl_)))
#> # A tibble: 1 × 4
#>       n median_sl q99_sl max_sl
#>   <int>     <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl>
#> 1 22588       152   1948  63103
```
:::


### Your turn

**1a.** Plot the distribution of step lengths and of turning angles.
**1b.** What does the turning-angle distribution tell you?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
par(mfrow = c(1, 3))

hist(st$sl_[st$sl_ < 3000], breaks = 60, col = "#1f6f78", border = "white",
     main = "Step length (< 3 km)", xlab = "metres")

hist(st$ta_, breaks = 40, col = "#1f6f78", border = "white",
     main = "Turning angle", xlab = "radians")

# A rose diagram respects the circular nature of the data
ta <- st$ta_[!is.na(st$ta_)]
brk <- seq(-pi, pi, length.out = 25)
cnt <- table(cut(ta, brk))
mid <- (head(brk, -1) + tail(brk, -1)) / 2
plot(0, 0, type = "n", xlim = c(-1, 1), ylim = c(-1, 1), asp = 1,
     axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "", main = "Turning angles (rose)")
r <- as.numeric(cnt) / max(cnt)
for (i in seq_along(mid)) {
  lines(c(0, r[i] * cos(mid[i])), c(0, r[i] * sin(mid[i])),
        col = "#1f6f78", lwd = 6)
}
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](exercise_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-5-1.png){fig-align='center' width=864}
:::

```{.r .cell-code}
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```
:::


**Step lengths** are strongly right-skewed: most steps are short (the animal
is resting or grazing), with a long tail of directed movement. This is why
step lengths are modelled with a gamma or exponential distribution, never a
normal one.

**Turning angles** peak sharply at 0 and again — more weakly — near ±π. The
peak at 0 is *directional persistence*: an animal that was heading somewhere
tends to keep heading there. The bumps near ±π are reversals, typically an
animal turning back within a patch, plus some GPS error at very short steps.

A uniform turning-angle distribution would mean no directional memory at all —
a simple random walk. Real animals are never that.
:::

## Task 2 — Scale dependence, demonstrated

Resample the *same* animals at four intervals and compare.

For turning angles we need a **circular** summary. The standard one is the
mean resultant length $\rho = \overline{\cos\theta}$: it is 1 for perfectly
straight movement and 0 for a uniform (memoryless) distribution.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
rates <- list(`1 h` = hours(1), `3 h` = hours(3),
              `6 h` = hours(6), `12 h` = hours(12))

scale_tab <- lapply(names(rates), function(nm) {
  tr <- resample_by_id(trk, rates[[nm]], minutes(15))
  s <- tr |> nest(data = -id) |>
    mutate(data = lapply(data, steps_by_burst)) |> unnest(cols = data)
  ta <- s$ta_[!is.na(s$ta_)]
  data.frame(rate = nm, n_steps = nrow(s),
             median_sl_m = round(median(s$sl_)),
             rho = round(mean(cos(ta)), 3),
             frac_straight = round(mean(abs(ta) < pi / 4), 3))
}) |> bind_rows()

scale_tab
#>   rate n_steps median_sl_m   rho frac_straight
#> 1  1 h   22596         152 0.258         0.416
#> 2  3 h    7567         472 0.294         0.423
#> 3  6 h    4002         887 0.223         0.393
#> 4 12 h    2011        1500 0.048         0.290
```
:::


For reference, a memoryless walk would give `rho = 0` and
`frac_straight = 0.25`.

### Your turn

**2a.** What happens to median step length as the interval grows?
**2b.** What happens to directional persistence — and is it monotonic?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution

**Step length increases**, from ~150 m at 1 h to ~1.5 km at 12 h — but far
less than proportionally. Twelve times the interval buys only about ten times
the displacement, because the path doubles back on itself. If movement were
perfectly directed the relationship would be linear; the shortfall *is* the
tortuosity.

**Directional persistence collapses**, but not smoothly:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
barplot(scale_tab$median_sl_m, names.arg = scale_tab$rate, col = "#1f6f78",
        border = "white", ylab = "Median step length (m)",
        xlab = "Sampling interval", main = "Step length grows with interval")
barplot(scale_tab$rho, names.arg = scale_tab$rate, col = "#b8860b",
        border = "white", ylab = expression(rho == bar(cos(theta))),
        xlab = "Sampling interval", main = "Persistence collapses by 12 h")
abline(h = 0, lty = 2)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](exercise_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-7-1.png){fig-align='center' width=816}
:::

```{.r .cell-code}
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```
:::


Persistence holds up to about 6 hours and has essentially vanished at 12
hours ($\rho \approx 0.05$, `frac_straight` ≈ 0.29 against the uniform 0.25).
So for these buffalo the timescale of directional memory sits somewhere
between 6 and 12 hours.

**The non-monotonic bit is the interesting part.** $\rho$ is *lower* at 1 h
than at 3 h. That is not biology — it is measurement. At an hourly interval
many steps are only a few tens of metres (a resting or grazing animal), and
when the step is comparable to the GPS error the *direction* of that step is
largely noise. Randomised directions drag $\rho$ down.

Two practical consequences:

- A correlated random walk fitted at 12 h would report almost no correlation,
  and you would wrongly conclude the animal moves at random.
- At very fine intervals, turning angles are contaminated by positional error.
  This is why step-selection analyses (Class 8) are usually run at an interval
  where typical step length comfortably exceeds GPS error.
:::

## Task 3 — Net squared displacement


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
nsd_of <- function(d) {
  d <- d[order(d$t_), ]
  data.frame(t = d$t_, nsd = (d$x_ - d$x_[1])^2 + (d$y_ - d$y_[1])^2)
}

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))

cil <- nsd_of(trk_hr[trk_hr$id == "Cilla", ])
plot(cil$t, cil$nsd / 1e6, type = "l", col = "#1f6f78",
     xlab = "", ylab = "NSD (km²)", main = "Buffalo 'Cilla' — sedentary")

vul <- read.csv("data/vulture_leo.csv.gz") |>
  transmute(t = as.POSIXct(timestamp, tz = "UTC"),
            x = location.long, y = location.lat) |>
  filter(!is.na(x)) |> distinct(t, .keep_all = TRUE) |> arrange(t)
vt <- make_track(vul, x, y, t, crs = 4326) |> transform_coords(crs_to = 6933)
v <- nsd_of(vt)
plot(v$t, v$nsd / 1e6, type = "l", col = "#c1440e",
     xlab = "", ylab = "NSD (km²)", main = "Vulture 'Leo' — migratory")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](exercise_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-8-1.png){fig-align='center' width=864}
:::

```{.r .cell-code}
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```
:::


::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Reading these two plots

**Cilla** rises quickly to a ceiling and stays there, oscillating. That is the
signature of a **sedentary** animal with a bounded home range: once it has
explored its range, it cannot get further from the start.

**Leo** shows six clean cycles: a sigmoid rise (autumn migration), a plateau
(wintering), a sigmoid fall (spring migration), a plateau (breeding). This is
the textbook **migratory** NSD profile.

Note the CRS: Leo spans 47° of latitude, so no UTM zone works. EPSG:6933 is a
global **equal-area** projection — appropriate for continental-scale distances
and areas.

NSD is a one-line diagnostic and it should be the *first* plot you make for
any new track. It tells you immediately whether a home range is a meaningful
thing to estimate.
:::

## Task 4 — MCP and KDE


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
cilla <- trk_hr |> filter(id == "Cilla")

mcp95 <- hr_mcp(cilla, levels = c(0.5, 0.95))
hr_area(mcp95) |> mutate(area_km2 = round(area / 1e6, 1))
#> # A tibble: 2 × 4
#>   level what           area area_km2
#>   <dbl> <chr>         <dbl>    <dbl>
#> 1  0.95 estimate 263530861.    264. 
#> 2  0.5  estimate  75532553.     75.5

kde95 <- hr_kde(cilla, levels = c(0.5, 0.95))
hr_area(kde95) |> mutate(area_km2 = round(area / 1e6, 1))
#> # A tibble: 2 × 4
#>   level what           area area_km2
#>   <dbl> <chr>         <dbl>    <dbl>
#> 1  0.95 estimate 292203479.    292. 
#> 2  0.5  estimate  61180281.     61.2
```
:::



::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
plot(hr_isopleths(kde95)$geometry, border = "#1f6f78", lwd = 2,
     main = "Buffalo 'Cilla': MCP (grey) vs KDE (teal)")
plot(hr_isopleths(mcp95)$geometry, border = "grey40", lwd = 2, lty = 2, add = TRUE)
points(cilla$x_, cilla$y_, pch = 16, cex = 0.2,
       col = adjustcolor("black", 0.25))
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](exercise_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-10-1.png){fig-align='center' width=672}
:::
:::


### Your turn

**4a.** Which is larger, and why?
**4b.** What does the 50% contour represent?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution

The MCP is convex by construction, so it swallows any concavity in the
animal's actual use — here, areas it moved around rather than through. The KDE
can be concave and can even be disjoint, so it hugs the used area more tightly.

The **50% contour** is conventionally called the *core area*: the smallest
region containing half the probability mass of the utilisation distribution.
It is a convention, not a biological threshold — but it is far more
informative than the 95% boundary, because it shows where the animal actually
concentrates.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
bind_rows(
  hr_area(mcp95) |> mutate(method = "MCP"),
  hr_area(kde95) |> mutate(method = "KDE")
) |>
  transmute(method, level, area_km2 = round(area / 1e6, 1)) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = method, values_from = area_km2)
#> # A tibble: 2 × 3
#>   level   MCP   KDE
#>   <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1  0.95 264.  292. 
#> 2  0.5   75.5  61.2
```
:::

:::

## Task 5 — Show yourself the autocorrelation problem

If KDE assumed independence and our fixes are autocorrelated, then **thinning**
the data should change the answer systematically. Let us check.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
thin_every <- function(tr, k) tr[seq(1, nrow(tr), by = k), ]

thin_tab <- lapply(c(1, 2, 6, 12, 24, 48), function(k) {
  d <- thin_every(cilla, k)
  if (nrow(d) < 30) return(NULL)
  a <- hr_area(hr_kde(d, levels = 0.95))
  data.frame(every = paste0(k, " h"), n = nrow(d),
             kde95_km2 = round(a$area / 1e6, 1))
}) |> bind_rows()

thin_tab
#>   every    n kde95_km2
#> 1   1 h 3518     292.2
#> 2   2 h 1759     303.6
#> 3   6 h  587     330.8
#> 4  12 h  294     345.2
#> 5  24 h  147     378.9
#> 6  48 h   74     400.2
```
:::


### Your turn

**5a.** What happens to the KDE area as you thin?
**5b.** What would happen if the fixes were genuinely independent?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
plot(thin_tab$n, thin_tab$kde95_km2, type = "b", pch = 16, log = "x",
     col = "#1f6f78", lwd = 2,
     xlab = "Number of fixes (log)", ylab = "95% KDE area (km²)",
     main = "KDE area depends on how many fixes you kept")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](exercise_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-13-1.png){fig-align='center' width=624}
:::
:::


The estimate **is not stable** — and it drifts in a consistent direction. The
95% KDE area grows steadily as we thin, from roughly 290 km² at hourly
sampling to about 400 km² at 48-hourly, a **~37% difference for the same
animal over the same period**.

If the fixes were independent draws from a fixed utilisation distribution, the
KDE area would converge to a constant as $n$ grows — more data, less noise,
same answer. Instead the denser data give systematically *smaller* ranges,
because adding more *autocorrelated* fixes adds
almost no new information about the utilisation distribution while the
bandwidth selector behaves as though it does. The effective sample size is far
smaller than `n`.

This is precisely the problem AKDE was built to solve — and precisely why a
95% KDE from 8,000 hourly fixes is not comparable to one from 60 VHF fixes.
:::

## Task 6 — AKDE with `ctmm`

`ctmm` fits a continuous-time movement model first, then uses its
autocorrelation structure to weight the kernel estimate.

::: {.callout-warning}
Model selection is genuinely slow — minutes, not seconds. We thin to
6-hourly fixes here so it finishes during class. For real work, use the
full track and be patient.
:::


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(ctmm)

cil6 <- thin_every(cilla, 6)

mb <- data.frame(
  timestamp = cil6$t_,
  location.long = NA, location.lat = NA,
  individual.local.identifier = "Cilla"
)
# ctmm wants geographic coordinates; convert the UTM track back
ll <- sf::st_coordinates(
  sf::st_transform(sf::st_as_sf(cil6, coords = c("x_", "y_"), crs = 32736), 4326)
)
mb$location.long <- ll[, 1]
mb$location.lat  <- ll[, 2]

tel <- as.telemetry(mb, timeformat = "auto")

guess <- ctmm.guess(tel, interactive = FALSE)
fit   <- ctmm.select(tel, guess, verbose = FALSE)

summary(fit)
#> $name
#> [1] "OUF anisotropic"
#> 
#> $DOF
#>      mean      area diffusion     speed 
#>  15.55335  26.82906 232.67046 163.80052 
#> 
#> $CI
#>                                          low        est       high
#> area (square kilometers)          257.316665 391.034715 552.287368
#> τ[position] (days)                  3.169814   4.953404   7.740585
#> τ[velocity] (hours)                 1.487567   1.919526   2.476918
#> speed (kilometers/day)              9.828279  10.643243  11.457383
#> diffusion (square kilometers/day)   7.402496   8.453952   9.574215
```
:::



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ak <- akde(tel, fit)
summary(ak)$CI
#>                               low      est     high
#> area (square kilometers) 230.5808 350.4051 494.9032
```
:::


### Your turn

**6a.** Compare the AKDE estimate with the KDE estimate on the same thinned data.
**6b.** What does the confidence interval tell you?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
kde_same <- hr_area(hr_kde(cil6, levels = 0.95))$area / 1e6
akde_ci  <- summary(ak, units = FALSE)$CI / 1e6   # m² → km²

c(KDE_km2 = round(kde_same, 1))
#> KDE_km2 
#>   330.8
round(akde_ci, 1)
#>                        low   est  high
#> area (square meters) 230.6 350.4 494.9
```
:::


Two things to notice.

**The point estimate differs.** AKDE corrects for the autocorrelation that
classical KDE ignores, and for this animal it typically comes out larger.

**AKDE gives you a confidence interval, and it is wide.** That width is the
honest statement of how much your data actually constrain the answer. A single
number from classical KDE hides exactly that uncertainty — which is why it is
so easy to over-interpret small differences between individuals or between
years.

The model summary is also worth reading: `ctmm.select()` chose a movement
model (OU, OUF, IID…), and the "area" row of `summary(fit)` reports the
range-residency estimate. If the selected model has **no** range residency,
the animal is not exhibiting home-range behaviour and an AKDE area is not a
meaningful quantity — the software will tell you, which classical KDE never does.
:::

## Self-check

::: {.quiz}
You resample a track from hourly to 6-hourly and the mean turning angle
distribution becomes almost uniform. What does this tell you?

- [ ] The animal's behaviour changed
- [x] Directional persistence operates on a shorter timescale than 6 hours
- [ ] The resampling introduced an error
- [ ] Turning angles are always uniform at long intervals for all species

::: {.quiz-feedback}
Directional persistence is a **short-term** property of movement. At a
six-hour interval the animal has changed activity several times, so the
direction of one step carries almost no information about the next, and
turning angles approach uniform.

This is a statement about the timescale of the *behaviour* relative to your
*sampling*, not about the animal changing. It also matters practically: a
correlated random walk fitted at 6 hours will report almost no correlation, and
you would wrongly conclude the animal moves at random.
:::
:::

::: {.quiz}
`ctmm.select()` chooses an IID (independent, identically distributed) model
for your track. What does that mean for your home-range analysis?

- [ ] AKDE will be identical to KDE, so use whichever
- [x] The fixes carry no detectable autocorrelation — usually a sign your sampling is too sparse to resolve the movement process
- [ ] The animal has no home range
- [ ] The model failed to converge

::: {.quiz-feedback}
An IID model says the data show no detectable correlation between successive
positions. For a modern GPS track that is nearly always a symptom, not a
finding: fixes so far apart in time that the movement process between them is
unresolved.

In that regime AKDE reduces to something close to classical KDE — it has no
autocorrelation to correct for. The estimate is not *wrong*, but you should
say plainly that the sampling could not resolve the movement process, and be
cautious comparing it with estimates from denser data.
:::
:::
